summary: AresNav is a human-EVA planning tool for the Martian surface, built on real NASA mission data for Gale Crater and the lower slopes of Mount Sharp. It combines the HiRISE 1 m terrain model and orthoimage with MOLA regional topography, then computes slope, roughness, hazard and data-confidence layers with deterministic, tested code. Operators explore an interactive map, inspect any point's elevation and slope, view elevation profiles, plan traverses between sites, simulate life-support use during an EVA, and export mission reports. Every value carries its source, instrument, resolution and limitations, and missing data is reported as unavailable or UNKNOWN instead of being treated as safe. The goal is to help future astronauts and mission planners choose walking routes with clear evidence. AresNav is a research prototype, not a certified safety system.
details: AresNav started from a simple question: if astronauts one day walk across Mars, how would a planner decide where they can safely go, and how would they know how much to trust the data behind that choice? We built a planning tool for a suited astronaut's walking trip (an EVA) across Gale Crater and the lower slopes of Mount Sharp, using real NASA data: the HiRISE terrain model and orthoimage from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and MOLA topography from Mars Global Surveyor. We cut that data down to our study area and worked out slope, roughness, hazard and data-confidence layers from it, all with ordinary tested code rather than guesses from an AI model. In the app you can explore an interactive map, switch layers on and off, click any point to see its elevation and slope, look at elevation profiles, plan a traverse between a base and a destination, compare route options, simulate how much life support an EVA would use, and export a mission report as Markdown, Word or PDF. What matters most to us is honesty about the data. Every value shows where it came from, which instrument measured it, how detailed it is and what its limits are, and when something is missing the app says it is unavailable or UNKNOWN instead of quietly treating it as safe. We hope this helps future mission planners see what is known and what is not before they send people out on foot. We built the backend with Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj and Shapely, and the interface with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts, Zustand and three.js, backed by 140 backend tests and 69 frontend tests. We should be clear about the limits too: only three NASA datasets are fully integrated so far, other datasets such as the USGS geology map, THEMIS thermal data and MSL radiation measurements are catalogued but not yet used, and AresNav is a research prototype, not a certified astronaut safety system. AI tools (Claude by Anthropic) were used to help write code, tests and documentation for this project, and the team directed the design, reviewed the output and ran the tests.
